get across.verb type: action — dynamic and causative: you cause an idea to land (*she gets her ideas across in meetings*), and the progressive is normal — *I'm still not getting it across*. No stative or linking use.
get across.passive: **restricted.** Causative *get* fights the passive even where there is an object: *the point was finally gotten across* is possible but stiff, and Americans say *the point finally got across* instead. The object-less *the joke got across* has no passive at all.

get after.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, nagging a person (*my mother got after me for weeks*) and attacking a job (*let's get after it*); the progressive is at home in each — *somebody's getting after the landlord about the heat*.
get after.passive: **no.** ✗ *the landlord was gotten after about the heat* is not English, and *get after it* is a frozen idiom with nothing to promote: ✗ *it was gotten after*.

get ahead.verb type: action — dynamic. Both the *rise at work* sense (*she works two jobs just to get ahead*) and *get ahead of* (*we got ahead of the story*) describe progress being made, not a state held.
get ahead.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is no object to promote, and the prepositional passive fails too: ✗ *we were gotten ahead of on price*, ✗ *ourselves shouldn't be gotten ahead of*.

get along.verb type: action — dynamic, though the *be friendly* sense names a relationship that holds over time; the progressive still works (*they've been getting along better since the move*), and the *be on your way* sense lives only there: *I should be getting along*.
get along.passive: **no** — intransitive in all three senses. The other person arrives through *with*, never as an object: ✗ *my first boss was never gotten along with*.

get around.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: moving about (*he gets around town on an old bicycle*), evading (*their lawyers found a way to get around the ban*), and spreading (*word got around fast*).
get around.passive: **restricted.** Only the evasion sense has an object, and even there the passive is stiff: *the ban was gotten around by their lawyers* is possible, but *their lawyers got around the ban* is what people actually say. ✗ *town is gotten around by bicycle*.

get around to.verb type: action — dynamic; it names the moment a long-postponed action finally starts (*I finally got around to fixing the fence*), usually with an *-ing* form.
get around to.passive: **no.** The three-part verb refuses it: ✗ *the fence was finally gotten around to*, ✗ *my email was never gotten around to*.

get at.verb type: action — dynamic in the *reach*, *criticize*, and *tamper* senses (*the raccoons got at the trash*, *his manager is always getting at him*). The *be driving at* sense is a verb of meaning and lives almost entirely in the progressive: *what are you getting at?*
get at.passive: **restricted.** The tamper sense passivizes naturally — *the witness had been gotten at before the trial*. Elsewhere it is marginal or impossible: *the shelf can't be gotten at without a ladder* is stiff, and ✗ *what was being gotten at?* fails outright.

get away.verb type: action — dynamic verb of escape and departure (*two of them got away*, *we're trying to get away for a few days*). The fixed *there's no getting away from the fact* presents a truth rather than a movement.
get away.passive: **no** — intransitive; what you escape arrives through *from*, and the prepositional passive fails: ✗ *the office couldn't be gotten away from until eight*.

get away with.verb type: action — dynamic: doing something wrong and escaping the consequence (*he got away with it because nobody checked the receipts*).
get away with.passive: **no.** Despite the obligatory object, the three-part verb has no passive: ✗ *murder is gotten away with every day*, ✗ *lying to her twice won't be gotten away with*.

get back.verb type: action — dynamic: returning (*call me when you get back*), recovering something (*she never got her books back*), and the shouted imperative *get back — that wire is live*.
get back.passive: **no** in practice. The recover sense is causative *get*, which blocks it: ✗ *her books were never gotten back*, ✗ *every dollar was gotten back*. English keeps the active — *he got back every dollar he put in*.

get back at.verb type: action — dynamic verb of revenge (*she spread the story to get back at her ex*), often in the progressive: *he's just trying to get back at me*.
get back at.passive: **no.** ✗ *her ex was gotten back at*, ✗ *the coach was gotten back at by the players* — the pattern has no passive despite always taking an object.

get back to.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, promising a later answer (*let me check the calendar and get back to you*) and resuming a task or topic (*I should get back to work*).
get back to.passive: **no.** ✗ *I was never gotten back to about the refund*, ✗ *that question will be gotten back to at the end*.

get behind.verb type: action — dynamic: falling behind is a change of state (*we got behind on the rent in March*), and backing somebody is the moment support is thrown (*the union got behind the proposal*).
get behind.passive: **no.** ✗ *the proposal was gotten behind by the union*, and the *fall behind* sense has no object to promote at all.

get by.verb type: action — dynamic; it describes coping over a stretch of time, so the progressive is natural: *they're all just getting by*, *we got by for years without a car*.
get by.passive: **no** — intransitive; what you manage on follows *on* or *with*, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *one salary is gotten by on*.

get down.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: recording (*let me get the address down*), depressing (*the gray February weather gets me down*), ducking (*get down — someone's at the window*), and the dated *dance* sense (*the whole room got down*).
get down.passive: **no** in practice. Both transitive senses are causative *get*, which blocks it: ✗ *every word he said was gotten down*, ✗ *I am gotten down by February*. English says *don't let them get you down*, never a passive.

get down to.verb type: action — dynamic; it marks the moment serious attention begins (*let's get down to business*), and the object is often an *-ing* form: *he can't get down to studying*.
get down to.passive: **no.** ✗ *business was gotten down to*, ✗ *no real work was gotten down to before noon*.

get in.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: arriving (*the red-eye gets in at 6:15*), being admitted (*he applied to Michigan and got in*), submitting on time (*get your timesheet in by noon*), and being elected (*if she gets in, the whole board changes*).
get in.passive: **no** in ordinary American use. The submit sense is causative: ✗ *the timesheet was gotten in by noon* — say *I got it in with an hour to spare*. The other three senses have no object at all.

get in on.verb type: action — dynamic: joining something already under way (*he got in on the ground floor of the company*).
get in on.passive: **no.** ✗ *the deal was gotten in on by four other states*, ✗ *the group order can be gotten in on* — the three-part verb has no passive, common though the active is.

get into.verb type: action — dynamic and inchoative throughout: taking up a hobby (*he got into birding during the pandemic*), being admitted (*she got into her first-choice school*), and getting tangled up in something (*they got into a shouting match*). The fixed *what has gotten into him?* is frozen in the perfect.
get into.passive: **no.** ✗ *birding was gotten into during the pandemic*, ✗ *a shouting match was gotten into in the parking lot*, ✗ *the legal side won't be gotten into tonight*.

get off.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: leaving a vehicle (*we get off at the next stop*), finishing a shift (*what time do you get off?*), escaping punishment (*he got off with a fine*), and sending something out (*get the invoices off today*).
get off.passive: **restricted.** Only the *clear somebody* sense really passivizes, and even that is informal: *he was gotten off by a good lawyer* (Americans prefer the active *a good lawyer got him off*). ✗ *the bus was gotten off at the next stop*, ✗ *the package was gotten off before five*.

get off on.verb type: action — dynamic, but close to a verb of feeling, so the habitual present is its home: *he gets off on telling people they're wrong*, *some managers really get off on the power*.
get off on.passive: **no.** ✗ *the attention is gotten off on*, ✗ *the pressure of a deadline is gotten off on by her*.

get on.verb type: action — dynamic: boarding (*get on the bus at Sixth and Elm*) and making progress (*how are you getting on with the report?*). The *growing old / growing late* sense exists only in the progressive: *her father is getting on*, ✗ *her father gets on*.
get on.passive: **no.** ✗ *the bus was gotten on at the last stop*, and the fixed *get on somebody's nerves* refuses it too: ✗ *my nerves are being gotten on by that beeping*.

get on with.verb type: action — dynamic in the American *continue* sense (*let's get on with it — we're forty minutes behind*). The British *be friendly* sense names a relationship rather than an act, but still takes the progressive: *they're getting on better than anyone expected*.
get on with.passive: **no.** ✗ *the job was gotten on with*, ✗ *the meeting can be gotten on with now*.

get out.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: leaving (*we got out before the storm hit*), removing (*she got the stain out with club soda*), news slipping loose (*word got out that the store was closing*), and releasing (*they got the newsletter out a day late*). *Get out!* as disbelief is a frozen interjection.
get out.passive: **restricted at best.** *The newsletter was gotten out a day late* and *the stain couldn't be gotten out* are heard but stiff; the active is the American default. The *leave* and *become known* senses have no object and no passive: ✗ *it was gotten out that the store was closing*.

get out of.verb type: action — dynamic: dodging a duty (*he got out of jury duty with a doctor's note*), exiting (*get out of the car slowly*), and gaining from an experience (*what do you get out of volunteering there?*).
get out of.passive: **no** for the three-part verb: ✗ *jury duty was gotten out of with a doctor's note*, ✗ *the parking garage couldn't be gotten out of for an hour*. The separate pattern *get something out of somebody* does passivize, because there the object belongs to plain *get*: *not a word could be gotten out of him*.

get over.verb type: action — dynamic; recovering and overcoming are processes, so the progressive is natural: *she's still getting over the flu*. The fixed negative *can't get over* (*I can't get over how tall he is*) is stative — it reports amazement, not an action.
get over.passive: **no.** ✗ *the flu was finally gotten over*, ✗ *the funding problem still has to be gotten over*, ✗ *my fear of flying can't be gotten over*. The active is the only option.

get over with.verb type: action — dynamic: finishing something unpleasant so it is behind you (*let's just get it over with*, *she got the hardest chapter over with first*).
get over with.passive: **no.** ✗ *the exam was gotten over with before lunch* — the frame demands an active with the object wedged between *get* and *over*: *get the dentist over with*.

get through.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: surviving a stretch (*I don't know how we got through that winter*), reaching somebody by phone (*I called nine times and never got through*), pushing a measure past a hurdle (*they got the bill through*), and consuming (*the four of them got through two pizzas*).
get through.passive: **restricted.** Only the *push a measure through* sense is anywhere near natural, and even there the plain intransitive wins: *the permit finally got through* over *the permit was finally gotten through*. ✗ *that winter was gotten through*, ✗ *two pizzas were gotten through*.

get through to.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, making somebody finally understand (*nothing I say gets through to him*) and reaching them by phone (*it took an hour to get through to an actual person*).
get through to.passive: **no.** ✗ *he is never gotten through to*, ✗ *the billing department couldn't be gotten through to*.

get to.verb type: action — dynamic: arriving (*we got to Tulsa by three*) and wearing on somebody (*the noise is starting to get to me*). The *have the chance to* sense is a **semi-modal** — *get to* plus a bare verb, marking permission or luck (*the kids get to stay up on Fridays*) — and it has no imperative and no passive.
get to.passive: **no.** ✗ *Tulsa was gotten to by three*, ✗ *I am being gotten to by the noise*, ✗ *she was gotten to meet at the signing* — none of the four senses passivize.

get together.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: meeting (*let's get together next week*), assembling (*can you get the receipts together by Friday?*), pulling yourself together (*he finally got it together*), and pairing off (*they got together in college*).
get together.passive: **no** in practice — the assemble sense is causative *get*: ✗ *the receipts were gotten together by Friday*, ✗ *they were gotten together in one folder*. The meet and couple senses take no object at all.

get up.verb type: action — dynamic: rising (*I get up at five*), rousing somebody else (*could you get me up at six?*), and summoning nerve or speed (*he never got up the nerve to ask her*).
get up.passive: **no.** ✗ *I was gotten up at six*, ✗ *the whole house was gotten up before dawn*, ✗ *the nerve was never gotten up* — the causative and the fixed-object senses both refuse it.

get up to.verb type: action — dynamic: being up to something, usually mischief (*what have those two been getting up to?*), and reaching a point in a sequence (*the bidding got up to four thousand*). Chiefly British; the American frame drops *get*.
get up to.passive: **no.** ✗ *all sorts of trouble was gotten up to at boarding school*, ✗ *chapter nine was gotten up to before the term ended*.

give away.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: donating (*the church gave away two hundred turkeys*), revealing (*his face gave him away*), losing an advantage (*they gave away a three-goal lead*), and presenting the bride (*her uncle gave her away*).
give away.passive: **yes**, and it is ordinary in every sense: *two hundred turkeys were given away*, *the ending was given away in the first review*, *a three-goal lead was given away in eleven minutes*, *she was given away by her uncle*.

give back.verb type: action — dynamic: returning an object (*give me my keys back*), restoring something abstract (*the surgery gave him back his sight*), and the object-less community sense (*she wanted a job where she could give back*).
give back.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *every cent was given back*, *his sight was given back to him after the surgery*. The community sense is intransitive and has no passive at all.

give in.verb type: action — dynamic; it names the moment resistance ends (*after two hours of arguing he gave in*), and *give in to* covers yielding to a feeling or a demand (*I gave in to the craving*).
give in.passive: **no** — intransitive in American use, so there is nothing to promote. The prepositional passive is marginal at best (?*their demands were finally given in to*), and ✗ *the craving was given in to* is not what anyone says.

give off.verb type: action — dynamic emission of heat, light, or smell (*the heater gives off a burning smell for the first minute*), though with a permanent property it reads almost statively: *those bulbs give off almost no heat*. The informal impression sense is the same pattern applied to people.
give off.passive: **restricted.** Natural in scientific and technical writing — *heat is given off during the reaction* — but stilted in everyday use (?*a sour smell was given off by the marsh*), and the impression sense refuses it: ✗ *the impression that he'd rather be elsewhere is given off by him*.

give onto.verb type: **stative** — a fixed property of a window, a door, or a room rather than anything done: *both bedrooms give onto the garden*. It rejects the progressive: ✗ *both bedrooms are giving onto the garden*.
give onto.passive: **no.** Like other stative verbs it refuses the passive even though it always takes an object: ✗ *the garden is given onto by both bedrooms*, ✗ *a small courtyard is given onto by the kitchen window*.

give out.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: distributing (*volunteers gave out water at mile six*), failing (*his knees gave out on the last flight of stairs*), running out (*our water gave out on the second day*), and releasing information (*they won't give out customer numbers*).
give out.passive: **restricted** — **yes** in the distribute and release senses: *water was given out at mile six*, *customer numbers are not given out over the phone*. **No** in the *fail* and *run out* senses, which are intransitive: ✗ *his knees were given out*, ✗ *our water was given out on the second day*.

give over.verb type: action — dynamic: handing control to somebody (*he gave the business over to his daughter*) and devoting a space or a stretch of time to a single use (*the basement is given over to storage*). The British imperative *give over!* is frozen and has no American currency.
give over.passive: **yes** — and the *devote* sense practically lives in the passive: *the whole basement is given over to storage*, *most of the hour was given over to questions*. The surrender sense passivizes too: *the land was given over to the county in 1974*.

give up.verb type: action — dynamic in all five senses (quitting, surrendering a seat, turning yourself in); the applause formula *Give it up for the band* is a fixed imperative, not a separate class
give up.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the habit was given up in 2019*, *his seat was given up to an older woman*, *the weapons were given up at the county line*. None for the intransitive *don't give up*, and the reflexive resists it: ✗ *he was given up by himself*.

give up on.verb type: action — dynamic, but it names a change of attitude rather than an act, so the progressive is limited to *I'm giving up on this*
give up on.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive works best with no agent: *by tenth grade she had been given up on*. With a *by*-phrase it turns clumsy: ?*she was given up on by her teachers*.

go about.verb type: action — dynamic in both American senses: tackling a task a certain way, and carrying on with your routine
go about.passive: **no** — *go* stays intransitive and the object belongs to the preposition: ✗ *the repair was gone about the wrong way*, ✗ *their business was gone about as usual*.

go after.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses (chase on foot, pursue a job or a record, attack in print)
go after.passive: **no** — the object sits behind a preposition and will not front: ✗ *the mayor was gone after for weeks*, ✗ *the record was gone after all season*.

go against.verb type: action — dynamic when you defy something (*he went against his father's advice*); closer to **stative** in *it goes against everything she believes* and *nothing in the report goes against the findings*, where the progressive is odd: ✗ *it is going against everything she believes*
go against.passive: **no** — ✗ *his father's advice was gone against*, ✗ *the tenants were gone against by the ruling*. Say *the ruling favored the landlord* instead.

go ahead.verb type: action — dynamic; the bare *Go ahead* is the same dynamic verb used as an imperative granting permission
go ahead.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the wedding was gone ahead*, and *go ahead with* keeps its object behind the preposition: ✗ *the renovation was gone ahead with*.

go along.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 1 lives almost entirely inside the adverbial *as we go along*, sense 2 means tagging along with someone
go along.passive: **no** — intransitive in both senses: ✗ *the rules were made up as they were gone along*, ✗ *he was gone along with to keep him company*.

go along with.verb type: action — dynamic; it reports a decision to accept, so the progressive is uncommon outside *I'm going along with it for now*
go along with.passive: **no** — ✗ *the recommendation was gone along with by the board*. American English says *the recommendation was accepted*.

go around.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: circulating illnesses and stories, detours, and *go around telling people that*; the *be enough* sense is fixed in *enough … to go around*
go around.passive: **no** — intransitive, and nothing promotes even when a route follows: ✗ *the block was gone around*, ✗ *the office was gone around by something*.

go at.verb type: action — dynamic and forceful in all three senses; the progressive is its home ground: *they were still going at it when I left*
go at.passive: **no** — ✗ *the problem was gone at for six hours*, ✗ *the yard was gone at with a machete*.

go away.verb type: action — dynamic when a person leaves, and still dynamic, but a gradual change of state, when a headache or a lawsuit goes away
go away.passive: **no** — intransitive: ✗ *the headache was gone away*. *Gone away* is only the perfect: *they have gone away for the weekend*.

go back.verb type: action — dynamic in the returning sense; **stative** in *the building goes back to 1890* and *he and I go back a long way*, which reject the progressive: ✗ *the building is going back to 1890*
go back.passive: **no** — intransitive in every sense, with the destination behind *to*: ✗ *the school was gone back to at forty*.

go back on.verb type: action — dynamic; it names one act of breaking a promise, so the simple past and the perfect dominate: *I've never gone back on a promise*
go back on.passive: **no** — ✗ *his word was gone back on within a week*, ✗ *the deal was gone back on*. English switches verbs: *the deal was broken*.

go by.verb type: action — dynamic when time passes or you swing past the store; **stative**-leaning in *go by the rules* and *he goes by Sully*, which state a standing fact rather than an act
go by.passive: **no** — ✗ *three years were gone by*, ✗ *the photos shouldn't be gone by*. *Gone by* survives only as an adjective: *in days gone by*.

go down.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense (falling prices, a crashed server, a setting sun, a prison sentence); **linking**-like in *it will go down as the worst season*, where *as* brings a complement, not an object
go down.passive: **no** — intransitive throughout: ✗ *the network was gone down at nine*, ✗ *eight years were gone down for*.

go down on.verb type: action — dynamic; vulgar sexual slang, and it belongs to no other class
go down on.passive: **no** — ✗ *he was gone down on*. The idiom stays active in every register that uses it at all.

go for.verb type: action — dynamic when you choose, when a dog lunges, or when a house sells; **stative** in *that goes for you too* and *I don't go for horror movies*: ✗ *that is going for you too*
go for.passive: **no** — ✗ *the salmon was gone for*, ✗ *the mail carrier was gone for by the dog*. Only *the house sold for well over asking* rescues sense 4.

go in for.verb type: **stative** — it reports a standing disposition, not an act, and resists the progressive: ✗ *he isn't going in for small talk*
go in for.passive: **no** — stative and prepositional at once: ✗ *long walks are gone in for*, ✗ *small talk isn't gone in for by him*.

go into.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: entering a profession, treating a subject at length, time and money spent, and falling into a state (*went into a skid*)
go into.passive: **restricted** — only the *treat at length* sense allows a stiff, formal prepositional passive: *the whole history has been gone into elsewhere*. The others have none: ✗ *medicine was gone into by both her kids*, ✗ *labor was gone into on the highway*.

go off.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: guns, alarms, sudden departures, an event that comes off well, and lights switching off
go off.passive: **no** — intransitive: ✗ *the gun was gone off*, ✗ *the event was gone off without a hitch*.

go off on.verb type: action — dynamic; a sudden outburst, so the simple past carries most of its uses: *he went off on the waiter*
go off on.passive: **no** — ✗ *the waiter was gone off on*, ✗ *the referee was gone off on by the coach*. American speech says *he got yelled at* instead.

go on.verb type: action — dynamic; the *happen* sense lives in the progressive (*what's going on?*), and *something to go on* is fixed after a quantity word
go on.passive: **no** — intransitive: ✗ *the meeting was gone on for three hours*, ✗ *his knee surgery is gone on about*.

go out.verb type: action — dynamic in all five senses; *go out with* is the dating frame and leaves the verb intransitive
go out.passive: **no** — intransitive: ✗ *the candles were gone out in the draft*, ✗ *he was gone out with for two years*. Sense 4 already reads as a passive without it: *the invitations went out Monday*.

go over.verb type: action — dynamic when you review, exceed a budget, or cross a pass; the *be received* sense (*the joke didn't go over well*) is dynamic too, but demands a manner word
go over.passive: **restricted** — the review sense takes a prepositional passive: *the numbers had been gone over twice before the meeting*. The others refuse it: ✗ *the budget was gone over by nine thousand dollars*, ✗ *the joke was gone over well*.

go through.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: enduring a hard stretch, searching, using up supplies, rehearsing, and a sale that clears
go through.passive: **restricted** — natural in the search sense: *every drawer in the house had been gone through*. Not in the others: ✗ *chemo was gone through last spring*, ✗ *a gallon of milk is gone through daily*; the *be approved* sense is intransitive already.

go through with.verb type: action — dynamic; it names carrying out a decision you had second thoughts about, and the object is nearly always *it* or an event noun
go through with.passive: **no** — ✗ *the wedding was gone through with*, ✗ *the surgery was gone through with after all*. Use *the surgery went ahead* instead.

go under.verb type: action — dynamic; each sense names a change of state — a business fails, a boat sinks, a patient loses consciousness
go under.passive: **no** — intransitive: ✗ *the company was gone under before the loan cleared*.

go up.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses; *go up in flames* and *go up in smoke* are fixed with that complement
go up.passive: **no** — intransitive: ✗ *the rent was gone up in June*, ✗ *she was gone up to and introduced to*.

go with.verb type: action — dynamic when you settle on an option or accompany someone (*let's go with the blue one*); **stative** in the matching and included-with senses, which reject the progressive: ✗ *that tie isn't going with the shirt*, ✗ *a parking space is going with the apartment*
go with.passive: **no** — ✗ *the local contractor was gone with*, ✗ *the fish is gone with by a dry white*. Say *we chose the local contractor*.

go without.verb type: action — dynamic; it covers a stretch of doing without, so the past and perfect are its usual tenses: *they went without heat for a week*
go without.passive: **no** — ✗ *heat was gone without for a week*, ✗ *lunch was gone without*. The object is optional anyway: *I'll go without*.

grind away.verb type: action — dynamic and durative in both senses; the progressive is its natural home: *they've been grinding away since seven this morning*
grind away.passive: **restricted** — the transitive *wear away* sense passivizes cleanly: *two decades of rust were ground away in an afternoon*. The *keep working* sense is intransitive and has none: ✗ *the dissertation was ground away at for six years*.

grind down.verb type: action — dynamic, and gradual in both senses, so the progressive suits it: *the lawsuit was grinding him down*
grind down.passive: **yes** — *he was ground down by four years of litigation*, *her molars had been ground down by years of chewing ice*.

grind on.verb type: action — dynamic and durative; it names a tedious continuation, at home in both the simple past and the progressive: *negotiations have been grinding on since March*
grind on.passive: **no** — intransitive: ✗ *the hearing was ground on into a third week*.

grind out.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: producing on schedule, winning ugly, and stubbing out a cigarette
grind out.passive: **yes** — *two columns a week are ground out on deadline*, *a 3-1 win was ground out in the rain*, *the cigarette was ground out on the step*.

grow apart.verb type: action — dynamic, but a slow process rather than an event, so the progressive fits: *they were growing apart for years before anyone said so*
grow apart.passive: **no** — intransitive, and it takes a joint or plural subject: ✗ *the brothers were grown apart*, ✗ *he was grown apart from*.

grow back.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 1 is a process the subject undergoes (*his hair grew back*), sense 2 an act with an object (*he grew the beard back by August*)
grow back.passive: **restricted** — acceptable only in generic statements about what can regrow: *a tail can be grown back; a finger cannot*. Awkward for a real event: ✗ *the beard was grown back by August*, and sense 1 is intransitive with no passive at all.

grow into.verb type: action — dynamic; every sense is a gradual development, which is why the perfect is so common: *he has grown into a careful, patient teacher*
grow into.passive: **no** — ✗ *the coat will be grown into*, ✗ *the job was grown into in about a year*. Say *she settled into the job*.

grow on.verb type: action — dynamic but gradual, with the thing as subject and the person as object; the progressive works: *the town is growing on me*
grow on.passive: **no** — the experiencer has to stay the object: ✗ *I was grown on by the album*, ✗ *everybody in the office has been grown on*. English says *I came to like it*.

grow out of.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1 and 2 (outgrowing boots, outgrowing tantrums); **stative** in sense 3, a standing fact of origin: ✗ *the company is growing out of a college project*
grow out of.passive: **no** — ✗ *those boots were grown out of in one winter*, ✗ *a college project was grown out of by the company*.

grow up.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses; the imperative *Grow up!* is a rebuke, not a separate class, and *grown up* in *she's all grown up* is an adjective, not a passive participle
grow up.passive: **no** — intransitive: ✗ *Cleveland was grown up outside of*, ✗ *the mill was grown up around*. Raising a child uses another verb: *she was brought up in Ohio*.
